comparison: Perfect agreement on study design and cell line classification (C25-C33). Both evaluations support the methodological approach, with peer reviewers explicitly praising the comprehensive panel assembly and proper controls. OpenEval notes the limitation of using site of collection rather than functional metastatic capacity, which peer reviewers do not critique.

Perfect agreement on transcriptome PCA results (C53-C57). Both evaluations support the EMT ordering in transcriptome space and the proximity of MDA-MB-231 to lung cancer cells. Peer reviewers implicitly accept these findings as part of the broader concordance/divergence analysis between compartment and transcriptomic changes.

Perfect agreement on brain metastasis control analysis (C73-C76, C98). Both evaluations strongly support this finding as validation of the organotropism hypothesis. Peer reviewers explicitly praise the prostate cancer brain metastasis comparison as successful validation, while OpenEval emphasizes its role as both negative control for breast cancer and positive control for specificity.

Strong agreement on PCA/EMT gradient findings (C41-C52, C86, C95). Both evaluations support the EMT gradient along PC1 and GO term enrichment. OpenEval includes C43 and C51 which peer review addresses separately. OpenEval notes PC2/HER2 association is more tentative, while peer reviewers accept the HER2 separation without qualification.

Strong agreement on independence of compartment and expression changes (C59-C65, C89-C91, C96). Both evaluations treat this as a novel and important observation. OpenEval notes the functional interpretation (C64-C65) remains speculative and would benefit from validation, while peer reviewers accept these interpretations without requesting additional evidence (addressed in R10).

Strong agreement on background/introduction claims (C1-C17, C18-C24, C101-C102). Both evaluations accept these as established facts supported by appropriate citations. Peer reviewers praise the citation of relevant references in 3D genome organization and EMT. OpenEval groups these separately (R1 and R2) while peer review addresses them together.

Strong agreement on organotropism/lung-permissive changes (C66-C72, C81, C84, C97, C99). Both evaluations strongly support this central finding. Peer reviewers call this 'the most important observation' while OpenEval provides detailed support but notes the study cannot determine timing of changes (primary site vs. metastatic adaptation). OpenEval includes C81 which peer review addresses separately (R9).

Strong agreement on hierarchical clustering results (C34-C40, C77-C80). Both evaluations support the clustering patterns and HER2/EMT-based separation. OpenEval includes C78-C80 (heterogeneity observation) which peer review addresses separately (R8). Both note the MDA-MB-231/lung cancer clustering supports organotropism, though OpenEval emphasizes causality cannot be established from clustering alone.

Strong agreement on main conclusions (C85, C94, C100). Both evaluations support the overall conclusions with peer reviewers calling this 'solid evidence with significant biomedical implications.' OpenEval includes C87-C88 which peer review addresses separately (R14). OpenEval emphasizes the causal role remains correlative and requires functional experiments, while peer reviewers accept the conclusions without this qualification.

Agreement on speculative mechanistic hypotheses (C82-C83, C92-C93), though evaluated differently. OpenEval rates these as UNCERTAIN, noting they are reasonable but untested hypotheses requiring experimental validation. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, accepting them as reasonable interpretations supported by citations. This represents a difference in evaluation stringency rather than disagreement on the data.

Both address speculative interpretations about lack of correlation between compartment and expression changes (C92-C93). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN requiring validation, while peer reviewers accept as reasonable hypotheses. Represents different standards for speculative claims rather than disagreement on observations.

Both address positioning relative to prior work (C87-C88). Peer reviewers accept this as valid extension of ovarian cancer work to breast cancer. OpenEval includes these in main conclusions evaluation, treating them as reasonably supported by the data showing concordant patterns across cancer types.

Both address lack of overlap between EMT and lung-permissive gene sets (C71-C72). Both evaluations support this finding as evidence for distinct regulatory processes. Peer reviewers accept without challenge, while OpenEval integrates this into broader organotropism analysis.

Both address functional interpretation of compartment/expression independence (C64-C65). OpenEval notes these interpretations remain speculative and would benefit from validation. Peer reviewers accept as reasonable hypotheses without requesting additional evidence. Represents different evaluation stringency.

Both address compartment shift patterns (C81). OpenEval includes this in organotropism analysis as a descriptive finding. Peer reviewers accept the observation and proposed mechanistic interpretations (C82-C83) without challenge. Minimal overlap but consistent acceptance.

Both address heterogeneity in clustering (C78-C80). OpenEval includes this in hierarchical clustering evaluation, noting it's consistent with cancer subtype characteristics. Peer reviewers accept without critique. Both treat as supporting observation rather than primary finding.

Both address 3D genome organization background (C18-C24). OpenEval evaluates these separately from other background claims as context for the study. Peer reviewers group all background claims together, praising citation of relevant references. Complete agreement on support.

Minimal overlap (C51 only). OpenEval addresses PCA results comprehensively while peer R1 focuses on clustering and HER2/EMT separation. Both support overlapping claims but organize evaluations differently, with OpenEval separating PCA from clustering analyses.
